text.en: It took me four months to finish Rick Rubin’s The Creative Act: A Way of Being. That’s a long time for me. The book has 78 areas of thought. My brand is 78. I had barely started reading and was already wondering what to make of that.  I’m skeptical of the idea that everything happens for a reason. But over those four months, I kept arriving at passages that spoke to whatever I was going through. After a breakup with someone I considered the love of my life, the passage about there being a season for everything gave me comfort. When I hit walls in my artistic practice, I found myself wondering what it meant to move in concert with the universe’s timetable.  The book’s opening made me think about the state of mind that makes art possible. Being an artist is something I practice in the way I pay attention, even on a day when I make nothing. I try to look at life as if I was born yesterday. I want to read slowly enough to be surprised when I read something again. I want to notice what I usually assume I already know. Last year I started calling this discovering rediscovery.  I see my own life as a work of creation. The way I perceive the world, what I give my attention to, and the choices I make all shape it. When I look deeper into the inner self, I see the outer world reflected there. I think of myself as a work of a creator, and I also wonder how that creator might be shaped by all of us.  I once found the same candy used in a Félix González-Torres installation at MoMA. I imagined setting up a candy installation in my studio and exchanging five pieces from each location. I was excited. When a visiting artist asked whether I understood what the work meant, that excitement gave way to doubt. How much do I need to know before I can follow an idea? Reading Rubin helped me recover my excitement. Sometimes an idea begins in play, and making it is how I find out what it can say.  Sometimes I don’t know what painting I’m making. I just start. The paintings I enjoy most are the ones I give no predestined destination. A rule can give me a place to begin. Questioning a rule can take me somewhere I didn’t know I could go. A mistake can bring something human into the work. An idea can feel smaller when it first becomes physical, and the practice of returning to it can stretch what I’m capable of making. Even if going somewhere unfamiliar changes who responds to the work, I want to keep the sense of discovery alive.  Don’t limit your work because the work wants to breathe. Don’t limit the breath of your work.  Rubin also made me think about developing my own sense of what makes work great. I’m still sitting with that one. I know innovation matters to me. I want to go beyond what I can already put into language and spend some time in the unknown. That takes experimental faith. Sometimes you have to believe you can do a thing before there’s any evidence you can. Then you try it, let it change, and see what takes shape. Be open to the universe editing the work.  I think of instinct as a direct conversation between me and the cosmos. I wonder what animals might sense before a natural disaster, and what we might notice if we were more attuned to what’s happening around us. I think about a child moving from one feeling to the next without embarrassment, a spontaneous move on a dance floor, or the impulse behind a mark in a Pollock painting. When I get quiet, an object in the room or a feeling in my body can spark an idea. It can feel like a whisper out of time, as if I’m listening from somewhere inside a much older stream. We know more than we can know. Feeling is the new seeing.  I also think about what artists owe other people. I made a hundred imitation BU ID cards to ask whether being public had become the default. Some of the people involved were strangers to me, and the project drew backlash. That response became part of what the work made me consider. Art can open a conversation by accident, and the people who encounter it get to bring their own experiences to it.  I was born into wealth and privilege. What do I do with it? Make Oxy. I want to build a space and a community where artists feel understood and have the freedom to express what they’re afraid to express. Fear can feel like touching the knob of a door I can’t see. I want artists to have the support to explore what’s on the other side, and I want audiences to feel free to find their own meaning there. Sometimes a work lets us recognize a feeling we rarely get to share. We feel less alone because someone gave it form.  Descartes wrote, “I think, therefore I am.” My version is “I question, therefore I am.” Publishing poetry books, holding exhibitions, and starting initiatives across communities are ways I’ve tried to give that question a life outside myself. A cave painting, Michelangelo’s David, and a child’s finger painting can all say “I was here.” What moves me is that someone else can encounter that trace and carry it forward. The work has a life in their hands, too.  Making art feels serious to me. I get to give an idea form and take part in a creation I already belong to. Making art also feels like pure play. I recognize myself in both. I’ve come to think of this as believing in a consideration rather than believing in a truth. I see through a keyhole. So does everyone who comes to the work. The contradictions I can see may be part of a pattern bigger than any story I can tell about it.  The last line I bookmarked was “The universe never explains why.”  I still can’t quite put into words what I felt when I read it. I do know what it gave me. The courage to do what I need to do and feel what I need to feel, even when I can’t explain why.

With privilege must come responsibility. Financial freedom gives me choices, and I feel a duty to use them to support my peers, take their dreams seriously, and contribute to cultural change. But how do I live out something I feel called to do while I’m still learning what that requires? Education matters. Yet where is the threshold for beginning? Some understanding emerges through action, through offering something and allowing others’ responses to change it. I have sprinted to create an ecosystem of opportunity. Now I want to slow down, do less with greater care, and give what I’ve begun time to develop. I believe opportunity, money, and dreams should keep circulating. I invite others with similar freedom to consider what they could make possible. My purpose is to help initiate change.
